tools.name: bash
tools.description:
Execute shell commands. Output is compressed by default; pass compressed: false for raw output. Piped commands run verbatim and show the pipeline's output; for AFT's test/build summary, run the runner without | head, | tail, or | grep. Pipeline-failure notes cover single top-level pipelines only; multi-statement commands (`a; b | c; d`) are not instrumented, so masked failures inside them still need explicit exit-code checks. Commands run in the foreground and return inline; wait: true blocks until a long command finishes instead of auto-promoting (it blocks up to bash.worker_wait_max_ms, 30 minutes by default, then reports the command is still running; watch again to keep waiting); Any new message detaches this wait. Set `bash.detach_on_user_message: false` to keep it blocking; even then, a message containing the literal `&detach` forces detachment, and the token is stripped before delivery and the rest of the message is preserved; a token-only message becomes `(requested background detach)`. Use it when you need the result before doing anything else; keep it off otherwise so auto-promote can remind you while you work. Use background: true yourself ONLY when you have other work to do while it runs, and any work that doesn't need this command's result counts; the task keeps running after the call returns, a completion reminder arrives when it exits, and bash_status reports its state and output. Use bash({wait:true}) instead when the result is needed before anything else. Do not change or delete files a background command uses until it finishes. A `nohup … &` launch still holds the call if the child keeps stdout/stderr; redirect both or use background:true. pty: true runs interactive programs (REPLs, TUIs), implies background, and is driven with bash_status({ outputMode: "screen" }) plus bash_write. Finished output expires after the task is 24 hours old and its completion has been delivered; under project-root restrictions, only the starting session can read output outside the project—copy cited lines into your report. `timeout` starts after spawn and kills the Unix process group (exit 124; Windows uses taskkill /T /F); processes that leave the group survive.

DO NOT use bash for code search or code exploration. If you are about to run grep, rg, sed, awk, find, or cat through bash to locate or read code: STOP — use the grep tool, read, aft_outline, or aft_zoom instead. When a list is cut, the reply ends with `shown N of M <unit> (<reason>) · narrow: <knobs>`; absence of that line means the list is complete.

command.description: Shell command to execute. Supports pipes, redirection, and normal shell syntax.

timeout.description: Hard kill cap in milliseconds (positive integer). In the default foreground mode when wait is false, a command that exceeds the configured wait window is promoted to background and gets a completion reminder when it exits; wait:true disables promotion and remains inline until completion, timeout, or bash.worker_wait_max_ms. A background task with no timeout is killed after 30 minutes; pass a longer timeout for long jobs.

workdir.description: Working directory for command execution. Relative paths resolve through the bridge; defaults to the current tool context/project root when omitted.

description.description: Short 5-10 word human-readable summary shown in OpenCode UI metadata instead of raw shell syntax.

wait.description: When true, run in the foreground without auto-promoting and wait until the command finishes or reaches its timeout (at most bash.worker_wait_max_ms, 30 minutes by default; the command then keeps running in the background and the reply says how to keep waiting); Any new message detaches this wait. Set `bash.detach_on_user_message: false` to keep it blocking; even then, a message containing the literal `&detach` forces detachment, and the token is stripped before delivery and the rest of the message is preserved; a token-only message becomes `(requested background detach)`. Use only when you know the result is required before doing anything else.

sandbox.description: Request one-command approval to run unsandboxed on the host; use only when native sandboxing blocks required work, and note that it is a no-op when sandboxing is disabled.

background.description: When true, spawn the command in the background and return a taskId for bash_status/bash_kill instead of waiting for completion. Defaults to false. A background task with no timeout is killed after 30 minutes; pass a longer timeout for long jobs.

compressed.description: When true or omitted, return compressed output with noisy terminal control sequences reduced. Set to false for raw output.

pty.description: When true, spawn the command in a real PTY for interactive programs (python/node/bash REPLs, vim). Implies background: true automatically. Inspect with bash_status({ taskId, outputMode: "screen" }) and drive interactively with bash_write — its input accepts either a string OR an array like [ "iHello", { key: "esc" }, ":wq", { key: "enter" } ] for atomic text+key sequences.

ptyRows.description: PTY terminal height in rows — ignored when pty is false. Defaults to 24 when pty: true. Minimum 1, maximum 60.

ptyCols.description: PTY terminal width in columns — ignored when pty is false. Defaults to 80 when pty: true. Minimum 1, maximum 140.

tools.name: read
tools.description:
Read file contents or list directory entries.

Use either startLine/endLine OR offset/limit to read a section of a file or sorted directory listing.

Behavior:
- Returns line-numbered content (e.g., "1: const x = 1")
- Lines longer than 2000 characters are truncated
- Output capped at 50KB
- Binary files are auto-detected and return a size-only message
- Supported images (PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP) and PDFs are returned as tool attachments; range arguments are ignored for media
- Directories return sorted entries with trailing / for subdirectories; offset is 1-based, limit defaults to and is capped at 1000 entries. Enumeration stops at 10,000 entries; partial listings carry a shown/total trailer.

Examples:
  Read full file: { "path": "src/app.ts" }
  Read lines 50-100: { "path": "src/app.ts", "startLine": 50, "endLine": 100 }
  Read 30 lines from line 200: { "path": "src/app.ts", "offset": 200, "limit": 30 }
  List directory: { "path": "src/" }

path.description: Path to file or directory (absolute or relative to project root)

startLine.description: 1-based line or directory entry to start reading from

endLine.description: 1-based line or directory entry to stop reading at (inclusive)

limit.description: Max lines (default: 2000) or directory entries (default and cap: 1000) to return

offset.description: 1-based line or directory entry to start reading from (use with limit). Ignored if startLine is provided

tools.name: write
tools.description: Write content to a file, creating it and parent directories automatically. Use `path` for the file location. Existing files are backed up before overwriting (undo via aft_safety). Auto-formats when the project has a formatter configured. Use it to create files or replace whole contents; for partial edits, use the `edit` tool. Write very large new files in parts: a single call can exceed the model's output limit and is then aborted with empty arguments.

path.description: Path to the file to write (absolute or relative to project root)

content.description: The full content to write to the file; for issue://N / pr://N, the comment body to post

tools.name: edit
tools.description:
Apply a hashline patch. Arguments are exactly `{patch}` where `patch` is a non-empty string. Server-owned preview control is outside this schema.

Quick reference:
- Header: `[path#TAG]`; TAG is exactly four hexadecimal digits from a current tagged read. Read every addressed row and gap boundary; REM and MV require a whole-file tagged read. Re-read after an edit before chaining: an edit-response tag can retain only changed context.
- Same canonical path: multiple sections compose in patch order against pre-request coordinates.
- Addresses: `0` (BOF), `N` (one line), `N.=M` (range; `N..=M`/`N..M` also work), `<N`/`>N` (gap before/after), `N*`/`<N*`/`>N*` (block), and `$`/`$-K` (EOF-relative). A plain `N` PUT replaces; use `<N` or `>N` to insert.
- PUT text: `PUT <address>:` followed by one or more `+` body rows (`+` alone is blank). A final patch newline is allowed. PUT without `:` copies `@name` (or the anonymous register) and takes no body; names use `@` plus ASCII letters, digits, `_`, or `-`.
- CUT: `CUT <address> [@name]`. REM: bare `REM` only, removing the whole file. MV: `MV <destination>` (one whitespace-free path, optional matching quotes), once and after any line operations. `*** Begin Patch`/`*** End Patch` is an optional envelope.
- Only `read` mint hashline tags. `aft_zoom`, `aft_outline`, `grep`, `aft_search`, and conflict snippets do not. After navigation, call `read` on every file and range the patch addresses.

patch.description: Hashline patch text with one or more [path#TAG] sections and PUT/CUT/REM/MV operations

tools.name: grep
tools.description: Search file contents using regular expressions. Returns matching lines with file paths and line numbers (no surrounding context lines — use `read` for that). Always case-sensitive. Lockfiles, generated and minified files, logs and command output, and JSON data files are counted, not printed, unless `path` or `include` names them; the reply lists them with the value to pass. Long lines are shown as a window around the match. A large result starts with matching lines per file and a 40-line first page; pass `offset` to page. When a list is cut, the reply ends with `shown N of M <unit> (<reason>) · narrow: <knobs>`; absence of that line means the list is complete.

offset.description: Rows of shown results to skip; follow the next offset the reply names.

tools.name: glob
tools.description: Find files matching a glob pattern. Returns matching file paths sorted by modification time. When a list is cut, the reply ends with `shown N of M <unit> (<reason>) · narrow: <knobs>`; absence of that line means the list is complete.

tools.name: aft_search
tools.description:
Search code with one tool: concepts, identifiers, error strings, regex, literals, and filenames are auto-routed to the right engine and returned ranked. For conceptual 'how does X work' queries, phrase a full natural-language sentence — the semantic lane is NL-aware and matches intent against docstrings and comments ('how does the ORM build and execute a query', 'where is rate limiting handled'), not just keywords. Exact names, strings, and regex stay terse ('^export', 'Cargo.lock').

When you know a name or string that must appear, put it in `pattern` (a regex, grep syntax, case-sensitive) and keep the question in `query`: both are ranked together, and the reply's first line says how many files the pattern matched and where it is defined. Example: query 'how is the config file loaded', pattern 'load_config|ConfigLoader'. `pattern` alone ranks the files it matches, definitions first.

Use `offset` to continue a ranked result list from a zero-based position.

When a list is cut, the reply ends with `shown N of M <unit> (<reason>) · narrow: <knobs>`; absence of that line means the list is complete.

query.description: Concept, regex, literal text, filename, or capability to find. Examples: 'fuzzy match with whitespace tolerance', '^export', 'Cargo.lock'. Optional when `pattern` is given.

pattern.description: Regex (grep syntax, case-sensitive) for names or text that must appear, e.g. 'load_config|ConfigLoader'. Ranked with `query` when both are given.

includeTests.description: Include test files (*.test.*, *_test.rs, __tests__/, …) plus test-support, fixture, mock, snapshot, and corpus files. Defaults to false.

path.description: Only set this to search a different project or plain folder (absolute or ~ path). Omit it for the current configured workspace, including non-Git workspace roots; this is not a subdirectory filter. Unindexed external folders use a bounded lexical fallback; filesystem roots, home and its ancestors are refused.

tools.name: aft_outline
tools.description:
Structural outline of source code, documentation files, or remote URLs. For code, returns symbols (functions, classes, types) with line ranges. For Markdown and HTML, returns heading hierarchy. Use this to explore structure before reading specific sections with aft_zoom. With `files: true`, the outline is breadth-first with directory rollups; drill in by outlining a subdirectory. Rows show language, symbol count, and line count.

For understanding a specific feature, prefer aft_search + aft_zoom on named symbols; use aft_outline on a whole directory only for high-level structure mapping. aft_zoom with `callgraph:true` gives one-level forward calls-out; use aft_callgraph only for reverse callers or multi-level traces.

Pass a single `target`:
  • file path → outline that file (with signatures)
  • directory path → outline source files under it
  • URL (http:// or https://) → fetch and outline a remote HTML/Markdown document
  • array of paths → outline multiple files in one call; with files:true, every path must be a directory

When a list is cut, the reply ends with `shown N of M <unit> (<reason>) · narrow: <knobs>`; absence of that line means the list is complete.

target.description: What to outline: a file path, directory path, URL, or array of paths. The mode is auto-detected: URLs by `http://`/`https://` prefix, directories by stat, arrays as multi-file.

files.description: Directory-only mode: when true, target must be a directory or array of directories and the result is a breadth-first file tree with directory rollups plus language, symbol, and line counts.

includeTests.description: Directory outline only: include test files. Defaults to false; tests are hidden.

tools.name: aft_zoom
tools.description: Inspect code symbols or documentation sections. Pass lookups in `batch: [{ target, symbols }]`; a single lookup is a one-entry batch. Mix files and URLs in one batch, for example `batch: [{ target: "src/app.ts", symbols: "run" }, { target: "https://example.com/docs", symbols: "Overview" }]`. Each target is auto-detected as a file path or an HTTP/HTTPS URL. `symbols` is a string or string array. Markdown and HTML lookups return the section under the heading. Top-level `contextLines` and `callgraph` apply to every entry; callgraph adds calls-out and called-by annotations. Each failed lookup reports its own error line.

batch.description: One or more lookups; entries may mix file paths and URLs

target.description: File path (absolute or project-relative) or HTTP/HTTPS URL, auto-detected; issue://N or pr://N when GitHub reads are enabled

symbols.description: Symbol name for code or heading text for Markdown/HTML; a string or array of strings

contextLines.description: Lines of context before/after each symbol (default: 3)

callgraph.description: Include call-graph annotations for every entry (default: false)

tools.name: aft_inspect
tools.description:
Codebase health inspection that waits for current analysis. FRESH means the reported analysis is current. PARTIAL means some diagnostics are unknown; the header names the analyzer, reason, and retry guidance. INTERRUPTED means the request stopped without a fresh snapshot; retry aft_inspect. PHASE-FAILED means inspection could not finish; address the reported reason and retry, or narrow the scope. `sections` selects drill-down detail. Scoped requests collect diagnostics when sections is omitted or includes 'diagnostics' or 'all'; sections that leave diagnostics out skip diagnostics work. Unscoped requests keep warm diagnostics. Categories switched off in `inspect.categories` are not computed or refreshed, render as off, and never make the header PARTIAL.

Use `scope=` to narrow all findings, counts, and examples to those paths. Cross-boundary duplicates are labeled as groups touching the scope. Scope also limits Rust analyzer startup to the Cargo workspaces owning those paths when diagnostics are requested. Files without an authoritative diagnostic report remain named gaps (complete: false), not a clean result.

Use when: starting work on unfamiliar code, after multi-edit batches to check diagnostics, before a refactor, before review, or to verify cleanup completeness.

Treat `dead_code` as a hint, not proof: reachability is call-based, so symbols reached only via method dispatch or referenced only in type position may be false positives — verify before deleting.

When a list is cut, the reply ends with `shown N of M <unit> (<reason>) · narrow: <knobs>`; absence of that line means the list is complete.

sections.description: Categories to include in detailed drill-down (e.g. 'todos' or ['todos', 'dead_code', 'cycles']). Use 'all' for every active category. Omit for summary-only mode. With scope, listing sections without 'diagnostics' (or 'all') skips diagnostics work; omitting sections keeps diagnostics. Other categories are verified regardless of sections.

scope.description: Restrict returned results to paths under this scope (one path, or an array of paths — not a space-separated list; file or directory; absolute or relative to project root). `scope=` narrows results. Scoped requests collect diagnostics for the scoped files and report coverage gaps, unless sections lists other categories and leaves out 'diagnostics'.

offset.description: Rows to skip independently in each drill-down list. Default 0; follow next_offset in each list envelope.

topK.description: Max drill-down items per category. Default 20, max 100.

tools.name: aft_callgraph
tools.description:
Answer code-relationship questions from a real call graph — instead of grep + read chains. Reach for this whenever the question is about how symbols connect: who calls X, what X calls, what breaks if X changes, how execution reaches X, or how a value flows.

Use aft_zoom with `callgraph:true` for one-level forward calls-out while reading source. Use aft_callgraph only for reverse callers or multi-level traces so you do not double-fetch the same relationships.

Ops:
- 'callers': Find all call sites of a symbol. Use before renaming or changing a function's signature.
- 'impact': What breaks if a symbol changes — affected callers with signatures and entry-point status (blast radius). Use before a risky edit.
- 'call_tree': What a function calls (forward traversal). Use to understand a function's dependencies before modifying it.
- 'trace_to': How execution reaches a function: each path of callers runs back to a root, labelled main, test, attribute, public API, or no caller found. Use to understand context around deeply-nested code.
- 'trace_to_symbol': Shortest call path from one symbol to another. Requires 'toSymbol'. If multiple targets match, the error returns candidate files; retry with 'toPath' to disambiguate.
- 'trace_data': Follow a value through variable assignments and function parameters across files. Requires 'symbol' (scope to trace from) and 'expression'.

All ops require both 'path' and 'symbol'. 'expression' is additionally required for trace_data; 'toSymbol' for trace_to_symbol.

Markers: ~ = edge resolved by name only (may point at the wrong same-named symbol); [unresolved] = callee not resolved to a definition, so the location shown is the call site. Unmarked edges are resolved exactly. By default, unresolved external/stdlib leaf calls in call_tree are collapsed into one summary per parent; pass includeUnresolved=true to show every unresolved edge individually.

When a list is cut, the reply ends with `shown N of M <unit> (<reason>) · narrow: <knobs>`; absence of that line means the list is complete.

path.description: Path to the source file containing the symbol (absolute or relative to project root)

symbol.description: Name of the symbol to analyze

depth.description: Max traversal depth (default: call_tree=5, callers=1, trace_to=10, trace_to_symbol=10 capped at 16, impact=5, trace_data=5)

expression.description: Expression to track through data flow (required for trace_data op)

toSymbol.description: Target symbol name for trace_to_symbol; the returned path ends at this symbol

toPath.description: Optional target file for trace_to_symbol; required when toSymbol exists in multiple files

includeTests.description: Include test files in callers/paths. Defaults to false; tests are hidden.

includeUnresolved.description: Show every unresolved external/stdlib call individually. Defaults to false; unresolved leaf calls are collapsed into one summary per parent.

tools.name: aft_conflicts
tools.description: Show all git merge conflicts across the repository — returns line-numbered conflict regions with context for every conflicted file in a single call. Conflicts are discovered from the git repository's top level. By default it inspects the session's project repository; pass `path` to inspect a different repository or git worktree (e.g. where a rebase/merge is running).

path.description: Optional path inside the git repository or worktree to inspect (absolute or relative to project root). Conflicts are discovered from that repository's top level. Defaults to the session project root.

tools.name: ast_grep_search
tools.description:
Search code patterns across filesystem using AST-aware matching. Supports 11 languages.

Use meta-variables: $VAR matches a single AST node, $$$ matches multiple nodes (variadic).
IMPORTANT: Patterns must be complete AST nodes (valid code fragments).
For functions, include params and body: 'export async function $NAME($$$) { $$$ }' not just 'export async function $NAME'.

Examples: pattern='console.log($MSG)' lang='typescript', pattern='async function $NAME($$$) { $$$ }' lang='javascript', pattern='def $FUNC($$$): $$$' lang='python', pattern='Writeln($MSG);' lang='pascal', pattern='$X <- $Y' lang='r', pattern='[obj foo:$ARG]' lang='objc'

pattern.description: AST pattern with meta-variables ($VAR, $$$). Must be complete AST node.

contextLines.description: Number of context lines to show around each match

tools.name: ast_grep_replace
tools.description:
Replace code patterns across filesystem with AST-aware rewriting. Applies changes by default — set dryRun=true to preview.

Use meta-variables in the rewrite pattern to preserve matched content from the pattern.
IMPORTANT: Patterns must be complete AST nodes (valid code fragments).

Example: pattern='console.log($MSG)' rewrite='logger.info($MSG)' lang='typescript' — replaces all console.log calls with logger.info across TypeScript files.

**Warning: This tool modifies files directly.** Use dryRun=true to preview (shows per-file unified diff, capped at 8KB). Consider creating an aft_safety checkpoint before bulk replacements.

pattern.description: AST pattern with meta-variables ($VAR, $$$). Must be complete AST node.

tools.name: aft_import
tools.description:
Language-aware import management. Supports TS, JS, TSX, Python, Rust, Go, Solidity, Java, C#, PHP, Kotlin, Scala, Swift, Ruby, Lua, C, C++, Perl, and Vue.

Ops:
- 'add': Add an import. Auto-detects group (stdlib/external/internal), deduplicates. Requires 'module'. Optional 'names', 'defaultImport', 'typeOnly'.
- 'remove': Remove an import or a specific named import. Requires 'module'. Provide 'removeName' to remove a single named import; omit to remove the entire import.
- 'organize': Re-sort and re-group all imports by language convention, deduplicate. Requires only 'path'. Use aft_safety checkpoint/undo for recovery before broad cleanup.

path.description: Path to the file (absolute or relative to project root)

module.description: Module path (required for add, remove — e.g. 'react', './utils', 'std::fmt')

names.description: Named imports to add. Each entry uses the language's native named-import text, including per-name aliasing where the language uses `as` (e.g. ['useState', 'debounce as db'], Solidity ['ERC20', 'IERC20 as IToken']).

namespace.description: Namespace binding: `import * as ns from 'mod'` (ES), `import * as N from "./X.sol"` (Solidity).

alias.description: Whole-module alias. Solidity: `import "./X.sol" as X` (module=path, alias=X).

modifiers.description: Statement-level modifier tokens, language-validated: Java/C# 'static'; C# 'global'/'unsafe'; Java/Kotlin/Scala 'wildcard'; Swift '@testable'. Unsupported tokens for the file's language return a clear error.

removeName.description: Named import to remove for 'remove' op; omit to remove entire import

validate.description: Validation level: 'syntax' (default) or 'full'. Syntax = tree-sitter parse check only. Full = also runs LSP type-checking (slower, catches more errors)

tools.name: aft_safety
tools.description:
File safety and recovery operations.

Per-file undo stack is capped at 20 entries (oldest evicted).

Ops:
- 'undo': Undo the entire last tool call when 'path' is omitted (typical), or undo the last edit to one file when 'path' is provided. Note: pops from the undo stack (irreversible, no redo). Use 'history' to inspect per-file history before undoing.
- 'history': List all edit snapshots for a file. Requires 'path'.
- 'checkpoint': Save a named snapshot (on disk across restarts; expires in 14 days; may contain secrets). Explicit files may be untracked/gitignored; omit for backup-tracked files. Requires 'name'.
- 'restore': Restore files to a previously saved checkpoint. Optional 'path'/'files' scopes the restore; omitted scope restores the whole checkpoint. Requires 'name'.
- 'list': List all available named checkpoints. No extra params needed.
- 'purge': Permanently delete this session's undo backups and checkpoint copies of 'path' (a file, or everything under a directory); cannot be undone.

Each op requires specific parameters — see parameter descriptions for requirements.

Use checkpoint before risky multi-file changes. Use undo for quick single-file rollback.

path.description: File path (required for history, optional for undo, optional for checkpoint — snapshots only that file when files is omitted, optional for restore — restores only that file, required for purge — a file or directory). Absolute or relative to project root

files.description: Specific files to include in checkpoint, or to restore from a checkpoint (optional; restore without path/files restores the whole checkpoint; explicit checkpoint files may be untracked or gitignored)

tools.name: bash_status
tools.description: Read-only snapshot of a background or PTY bash task's current state and output; a remote job ID works too. Returns immediately and never waits; the task keeps running, and a completion reminder arrives when it exits.

taskId.description: Background task ID returned by bash({ background: true }), e.g. bash-6b454047a1c39ded, or its remote job ID.

outputOffset.description: Read a bounded stdout/PTY byte page from this offset; returns masked text and the next byte offset.

stderrOffset.description: Read a bounded stderr byte page from this offset; returns masked text and the next byte offset.

outputMode.description: PTY output rendering mode. Defaults to screen for PTY tasks and preserves existing behavior for piped tasks when omitted.

tools.name: bash_kill
tools.description: Terminate a running background bash task spawned with bash({ background: true }); a remote job ID works too. Returns confirmation of kill or an error if the task already finished.

taskId.description: Background task ID returned by bash({ background: true }), e.g. bash-6b454047a1c39ded, or its remote job ID.

tools.name: bash_write
tools.description: Write input bytes to a running PTY bash task. PTY-only; check bash_status reports mode: "pty" first. Input is either a string (verbatim bytes) or an array mixing strings and { key: "esc" | "enter" | "up" | "ctrl-c" | ... } objects for atomic text+key sequences such as [ "iHello", { key: "esc" }, ":wq", { key: "enter" } ]. Named keys cover enter/return/tab/space/backspace/esc/escape, arrows, home/end/page-up/page-down/delete/insert, f1..f12, and ctrl-a..ctrl-z. Maximum 1 MiB per call (post-expansion).

taskId.description: Background PTY task ID returned by bash({ pty: true, background: true }).

input.description: Either a string of verbatim bytes (e.g. 'print(1)\n') OR an array mixing strings and { key: '<name>' } objects for atomic text+key sequences. Example: [ 'iHello', { key: 'esc' }, ':wq', { key: 'enter' } ].

system_text.text:
# Agent Foundational Toolkit

**Code exploration**: `aft_search` is the primary code-search tool: one call auto-routes concepts, identifiers, regex, error strings, and literals. Then `aft_outline` for structure → `aft_zoom` for symbol(s). DO NOT run `grep`/`rg`/`find`/`sed`/`cat` through `bash` to locate or read code — the bash path is unindexed, unranked, serial, and routinely surfaces the wrong hit. Keep `bash` for shell facts (git state, file metadata, processes). If you are about to run grep, rg, sed, awk, find, or cat through bash to locate or read code: STOP — use aft_search (concepts, identifiers, regex, literals), read, aft_outline, or aft_zoom instead. Reflex translations:
- `grep -rn "handleAuth" src/` in bash → `aft_search({ query: "handleAuth" })`
- `find . -name "*.ts" | xargs grep watcher` in bash → `aft_search({ query: "watcher invalidation" })` (concepts work too)
- `sed -n '100,160p' app.ts` / `cat app.ts` in bash → `read({ path: "app.ts", startLine: 100, endLine: 160 })`
**Relationships**: aft_callgraph for callers, impact, and execution or data-flow traces.
**Web pages**: aft_outline with a URL as target, then aft_zoom on a heading.
**Parallel calls**: send independent read-only calls in one response.
**After edits**: run aft_inspect for diagnostics; the project's typecheck and tests are the final check.
**Status bar**: `[AFT E.. W.. | T..]` appears when a count changes. E above 0 usually means your last edit broke something; `?` means unknown, not zero.
**Commands**: don't pipe test or build output into tail, grep or head; AFT already shortens it. Pass wait: true when you need a long command's result before anything else. Otherwise a long command moves to the background and a notice brings its result.
**Hashline edit tags**: Only `read` mint hashline tags. `aft_zoom`, `aft_outline`, `grep`, `aft_search`, and conflict snippets do not. After navigation, call `read` on every file and range the patch addresses.
